notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Petroleum is a naturally occurring complex mixture of hydrocarbons.
  • The word petroleum comes from Latin words meaning rock and oil.
  • Crude petroleum is also called crude oil.
  • Petroleum is a fossil fuel.
  • Petroleum is non-renewable on the human timescale.
  • Crude oil must be refined before most useful products are obtained.
  • Petroleum products include LPG, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and bitumen.
  • Petroleum is also a major raw material for the petrochemical industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Crude Petroleum → Hydrocarbon Mixture → Refining → Useful Fractions

2. Origin of Petroleum
  • Petroleum formed mainly from ancient marine organisms and organic matter buried under sediments.
  • Burial subjected organic material to heat and pressure over geological time.
  • Oxygen-poor conditions reduced complete decomposition.
  • Organic matter was transformed into hydrocarbons.
  • Petroleum formation requires millions of years.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petroleum → Ancient Organic Matter + Heat + Pressure + Time

3. Fossil Fuels

Important fossil fuels are:

  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • They formed from ancient biological material.
  • Fossil fuels are finite resources.
  • Their combustion releases carbon dioxide.
4. Petroleum Reservoir
  • Petroleum accumulates within porous reservoir rocks.
  • Impermeable cap rock can trap hydrocarbons.
  • Oil and natural gas may occur together.
  • Water is often present below the oil layer.
  • Geological structures such as anticlines can form petroleum traps.
5. Petroleum Trap

A typical petroleum accumulation may contain:

  • Natural gas at the top.
  • Crude oil below gas.
  • Formation water below oil.

This arrangement results largely from differences in density.

🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gas → Top

Oil → Middle

Water → Bottom

6. Crude Oil
  • Crude oil is petroleum obtained directly from underground reservoirs.
  • It may range from light to very heavy.
  • Colour can vary from yellowish-brown to black.
  • Crude oil contains many hydrocarbons with different boiling points.
  • It may also contain sulfur, nitrogen and oxygen compounds.
  • Trace metals may also occur.
7. Hydrocarbons
  • Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
  • Petroleum contains many hydrocarbon types.
  • Major classes include alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons.
  • Different hydrocarbons have different boiling points and properties.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydrocarbon → Carbon + Hydrogen Only

8. Alkanes
  • Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons.
  • They contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.
  • General formula for open-chain alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
  • Methane is CH₄.
  • Ethane is C₂H₆.
  • Propane is C₃H₈.
  • Butane is C₄H₁₀.
9. Saturated Hydrocarbon
  • Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms.
  • Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons.
  • They generally undergo substitution reactions more readily than addition reactions.
10. Unsaturated Hydrocarbon
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain one or more carbon-carbon double or triple bonds.
  • Alkenes contain double bonds.
  • Alkynes contain triple bonds.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons are important petrochemical feedstocks.
11. Aromatic Hydrocarbons
  • Aromatic hydrocarbons contain benzene-like ring systems.
  • Benzene has formula C₆H₆.
  • Toluene and xylene are important aromatic petrochemicals.
  • Many aromatic hydrocarbons are used in chemical manufacture.
  • Some aromatic compounds are toxic or carcinogenic.
12. Petroleum Exploration

Important exploration methods include:

  • Geological surveys.
  • Seismic surveys.
  • Exploratory drilling.
  • Well logging.
  • Geophysical analysis.
  • Seismic methods are especially important in locating subsurface structures.
13. Oil Well
  • An oil well is drilled into an underground petroleum reservoir.
  • Oil may initially flow because of reservoir pressure.
  • Pumps may later be required.
  • Water or gas injection may help maintain pressure and increase recovery.
14. Petroleum Refinery
  • A petroleum refinery separates and converts crude oil into useful products.
  • Fractional distillation is the first major separation process.
  • Additional processing improves product quality and yield.
  • Refinery processes include cracking, reforming, desulfurisation and blending.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Refinery → Separation + Conversion + Purification

15. Fractional Distillation
  • Fractional distillation separates crude oil according to boiling ranges.
  • Crude oil is heated.
  • Most of it vaporises.
  • Vapours enter a tall fractionating column.
  • The column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top.
  • Different hydrocarbons condense at different heights.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petroleum Refining → Fractional Distillation

16. Fractionating Column
  • Heavy fractions condense near the lower hotter part.
  • Lighter fractions rise higher before condensing.
  • Very light gases leave near the top.
  • Residual heavy materials remain near the bottom.
📌 Memory

Top → Light, low-boiling fractions

Bottom → Heavy, high-boiling fractions

17. Fraction
  • A petroleum fraction is a mixture of hydrocarbons having a similar boiling range.
  • A fraction is not generally a single pure compound.
  • Fractions differ in carbon-chain length, volatility and viscosity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Petroleum fraction ≠ One pure hydrocarbon.

18. General Trend in Petroleum Fractions

Moving from top to bottom of the fractionating column:

  • Molecular size increases.
  • Boiling point increases.
  • Viscosity increases.
  • Volatility decreases.
  • Flammability generally becomes less easy.
  • Colour generally becomes darker.
19. Refinery Gas
  • Refinery gases are among the lightest petroleum fractions.
  • They contain small hydrocarbons such as propane and butane.
  • They are used as fuel and petrochemical feedstock.
  • LPG is closely related to these gases.
20. LPG
  • LPG stands for Liquefied Petroleum Gas.
  • LPG mainly contains propane and butane.
  • It is stored as a liquid under pressure.
  • On release, it vaporises readily.
  • LPG is used for cooking, heating and industrial applications.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LPG → Propane + Butane

21. Why LPG Is Stored as Liquid
  • Propane and butane can be liquefied by moderate pressure.
  • Liquid occupies far less volume than gas.
  • This makes storage and transport convenient.
  • LPG cylinders therefore contain liquefied fuel under pressure.
22. LPG Odour
  • Pure LPG components are nearly odourless.
  • Odorants are deliberately added for leak detection.
  • Ethyl mercaptan or related sulfur compounds are commonly used as odorants.
  • The strong smell helps detect gas leaks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LPG Smell → Added Odorant

23. LPG Safety
  • LPG vapour is heavier than air.
  • Leaked LPG can collect near floors in poorly ventilated spaces.
  • LPG is highly flammable.
  • Cylinders must be protected from excessive heat.
  • Leak detection should not involve an open flame.
24. Petrol
  • Petrol is also called gasoline.
  • It is a volatile liquid fuel.
  • Petrol contains mainly hydrocarbons suitable for spark-ignition engines.
  • It is used primarily in petrol-powered vehicles.
  • Petrol evaporates more readily than diesel.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petrol Engine → Spark Ignition

25. Gasoline Fraction
  • Gasoline contains relatively low molecular-mass hydrocarbons.
  • Typical carbon numbers are roughly C₅ to C₁₂, though commercial fuels contain complex mixtures.
  • Petrol must have suitable volatility and anti-knock properties.
26. Naphtha
  • Naphtha is a petroleum fraction between gasoline-like and kerosene-like ranges depending on refinery classification.
  • It is an important petrochemical feedstock.
  • It is used to produce hydrogen, solvents and chemicals.
  • Steam cracking of naphtha produces important alkenes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Naphtha → Major Petrochemical Feedstock

27. Kerosene
  • Kerosene is a petroleum middle fraction.
  • It is less volatile than petrol.
  • It is used as fuel in some stoves and lamps.
  • Aviation turbine fuel is kerosene-based.
  • Jet fuel is specially refined and tightly specified.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kerosene → Aviation Turbine Fuel Base

28. Aviation Turbine Fuel
  • ATF stands for Aviation Turbine Fuel.
  • Commercial jet aircraft commonly use kerosene-type aviation fuel.
  • Jet fuel is not the same as automobile petrol.
  • Fuel properties are controlled for safety at high altitude and low temperature.
29. Diesel
  • Diesel is heavier and less volatile than petrol.
  • It is used in compression-ignition engines.
  • Diesel engines do not require a spark plug for normal ignition of the fuel-air mixture.
  • High compression heats the air sufficiently for injected fuel to ignite.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diesel Engine → Compression Ignition

30. Diesel Fraction
  • Diesel contains larger hydrocarbon molecules than petrol on average.
  • It has a higher boiling range.
  • It is less volatile.
  • It has greater energy content per litre than petrol in typical commercial fuels.
31. Gas Oil
  • Gas oil is a middle-to-heavy petroleum fraction.
  • Diesel fuel is produced largely from gas-oil fractions.
  • Some gas oil is used in heating and industrial applications.
32. Lubricating Oil
  • Lubricating oil is a heavy petroleum fraction.
  • It reduces friction between moving machine parts.
  • It reduces wear.
  • It helps carry away heat.
  • Lubricants may contain additives to improve performance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lubricant → Friction and Wear ↓

33. Lubricating Grease
  • Grease is a semi-solid lubricant.
  • It generally contains lubricating oil thickened with soap or another thickener.
  • It remains in place better than liquid oil.
  • Grease is used in bearings and machinery.
34. Paraffin Wax
  • Paraffin wax is obtained from heavier petroleum fractions.
  • It contains mainly long-chain saturated hydrocarbons.
  • It is used in candles, polishes, waterproofing and packaging.
  • It is a solid at room temperature.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Paraffin Wax → Candles

35. Petroleum Jelly
  • Petroleum jelly is a semi-solid mixture of hydrocarbons obtained from petroleum refining.
  • It is used in skin-protection products and lubricating applications.
  • Vaseline is a well-known trade name for petroleum jelly.
36. Fuel Oil
  • Fuel oil is a heavy petroleum product.
  • It is used in some industrial boilers, ships and furnaces.
  • Heavy fuel oils are more viscous than diesel.
37. Bitumen
  • Bitumen is a very heavy petroleum residue.
  • It is black and highly viscous.
  • It is used mainly in road construction and roofing.
  • It acts as a binder in asphalt mixtures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bitumen → Roads

38. Bitumen vs Asphalt
  • Bitumen is the binding petroleum material.
  • Asphalt is generally a mixture containing bitumen with mineral aggregates.
  • The terms may be used differently in different countries.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Bitumen and asphalt are closely related but not chemically identical terms.

39. Major Petroleum Fractions — Order

From lighter to heavier:

  • Refinery gases/LPG.
  • Petrol/gasoline.
  • Naphtha.
  • Kerosene.
  • Diesel/gas oil.
  • Lubricating oils.
  • Fuel oils.
  • Paraffin wax/heavy products.
  • Bitumen/residue.
📌 Must-Memorise

Top → LPG

Bottom → Bitumen

40. Boiling Range Trend
  • LPG components have very low boiling points.
  • Petrol boils over a relatively low range.
  • Kerosene has a higher boiling range.
  • Diesel boils higher still.
  • Lubricating oils and residues have the highest boiling ranges.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Molecular Size ↑ → Boiling Point ↑

41. Volatility
  • Volatility is a substance's tendency to vaporise.
  • Petrol is more volatile than kerosene.
  • Kerosene is more volatile than diesel.
  • Bitumen has extremely low volatility under ordinary conditions.
📌 Memory

Petrol > Kerosene > Diesel in volatility

42. Viscosity
  • Viscosity is resistance to flow.
  • Heavy petroleum fractions have greater viscosity.
  • Bitumen has very high viscosity.
  • Petrol has low viscosity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heavy Fraction → Viscosity ↑

43. Flash Point
  • Flash point is the lowest temperature at which a liquid produces enough vapour to ignite briefly when an ignition source is applied.
  • Petrol has a low flash point.
  • Diesel has a higher flash point than petrol.
  • Higher flash point generally makes storage less prone to easy vapour ignition.
44. Fire Point
  • Fire point is the lowest temperature at which vapour continues to burn after ignition under specified test conditions.
  • Fire point is generally above flash point.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Flash point → Brief ignition.

Fire point → Sustained burning.

45. Autoignition Temperature
  • Autoignition temperature is the temperature at which a substance ignites without an external flame or spark.
  • It is different from flash point.
  • Diesel-engine combustion relies on air being compressed until it becomes hot enough for injected fuel to ignite.
46. Petrol Engine
  • Petrol engines are usually spark-ignition engines.
  • A spark plug initiates combustion.
  • Petrol and air are mixed before or during intake depending on engine design.
  • Octane number is important for petrol quality.
47. Diesel Engine
  • Diesel engines are compression-ignition engines.
  • Air is compressed strongly.
  • Fuel is injected into hot compressed air.
  • Fuel self-ignites.
  • Cetane number is important for diesel ignition quality.
48. Engine Knocking
  • Knocking is abnormal combustion that produces rapid pressure oscillations.
  • Petrol-engine knock occurs when part of the fuel-air mixture autoignites undesirably.
  • Severe knocking reduces efficiency and can damage the engine.
  • Fuel anti-knock quality is measured using octane rating.
49. Octane Number
  • Octane number indicates resistance of petrol to knocking.
  • Higher octane number means greater resistance to autoignition knock in spark-ignition engines.
  • Iso-octane is assigned an octane number of 100 in the traditional reference scale.
  • n-Heptane is assigned 0 in the traditional reference scale.
📌 Must-Memorise

Iso-octane → 100

n-Heptane → 0

50. High-Octane Fuel
  • High-octane petrol is suitable for engines designed for higher compression or greater knock resistance.
  • Higher octane does not automatically mean greater energy content.
  • Using unnecessarily high octane does not inherently create more power in engines not designed to benefit from it.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Octane number → Knock resistance, not energy content.

51. Tetraethyl Lead
  • Tetraethyl lead was historically added to petrol to increase octane rating.
  • Leaded petrol caused serious environmental and health problems.
  • Lead additives have been phased out from road fuels in many countries including India.
  • Modern petrol uses other blending components and additives.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tetraethyl Lead → Historical Anti-Knock Additive

52. Cetane Number
  • Cetane number measures ignition quality of diesel fuel.
  • Higher cetane number means shorter ignition delay under test conditions.
  • It is important for compression-ignition engines.
  • Cetane is the historical high-quality reference compound.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petrol → Octane

Diesel → Cetane

53. Octane vs Cetane
  • Octane number measures resistance to premature autoignition in petrol engines.
  • Cetane number measures readiness for ignition in diesel engines.
  • High octane is desirable for spark-ignition fuel.
  • Suitable high cetane is desirable for compression-ignition fuel.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Octane → Petrol.

Cetane → Diesel.

54. Cracking
  • Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller molecules.
  • It increases production of useful fuels such as gasoline.
  • Cracking also produces alkenes used in petrochemicals.
  • Cracking may be thermal or catalytic.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cracking → Large Hydrocarbon → Smaller Hydrocarbons

55. Thermal Cracking
  • Thermal cracking uses high temperature and pressure.
  • Large hydrocarbons break into smaller alkanes and alkenes.
  • It was historically important before catalytic methods became dominant.
56. Catalytic Cracking
  • Catalytic cracking uses catalysts to promote hydrocarbon breakdown.
  • It operates under more controlled conditions than simple thermal cracking.
  • It produces high-quality gasoline-range hydrocarbons.
  • Zeolite catalysts are widely used.
57. Fluid Catalytic Cracking
  • FCC stands for Fluid Catalytic Cracking.
  • It is a major refinery conversion process.
  • Heavy gas oils are converted into lighter products.
  • Gasoline and light olefins are important products.
58. Hydrocracking
  • Hydrocracking breaks heavy hydrocarbons in the presence of hydrogen and a catalyst.
  • It produces cleaner lighter fuels.
  • It can help remove sulfur and nitrogen compounds simultaneously.
59. Reforming
  • Catalytic reforming rearranges low-octane hydrocarbons into higher-octane molecules.
  • It can produce aromatic hydrocarbons and hydrogen.
  • Reforming increases gasoline quality.
  • Platinum-containing catalysts are commonly used in reforming processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reforming → Octane Quality ↑

60. Isomerisation
  • Isomerisation rearranges straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched isomers.
  • Branched hydrocarbons generally have better anti-knock properties in petrol.
  • Isomerisation therefore helps increase octane quality.
61. Alkylation
  • Alkylation combines smaller hydrocarbons to form larger branched hydrocarbons.
  • The products can have high octane numbers.
  • Alkylation is important in petrol blending.
62. Desulfurisation
  • Crude oil and fuels may contain sulfur compounds.
  • Hydrodesulfurisation removes sulfur using hydrogen and catalysts.
  • Sulfur removal reduces sulfur dioxide emissions during combustion.
  • Low-sulfur fuels reduce air pollution.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fuel Sulfur ↓ → SO₂ Pollution ↓

63. Sweet and Sour Crude
  • Sweet crude contains relatively little sulfur.
  • Sour crude contains higher sulfur content.
  • Sweet crude is generally easier and less costly to refine.
  • Sour crude requires more desulfurisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sweet Crude → Low Sulfur

Sour Crude → High Sulfur

64. Refinery Blending
  • Finished fuels are usually blends of many refinery streams.
  • Additives may improve stability, cleanliness, lubricity or ignition properties.
  • Commercial petrol and diesel are therefore complex formulations.
65. Petrochemicals
  • Petrochemicals are chemicals obtained mainly from petroleum and natural gas.
  • They are raw materials for plastics, synthetic fibres, detergents, solvents and fertilisers.
  • Petrochemical industry converts hydrocarbons into thousands of products.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petroleum → Fuel + Petrochemical Raw Material

66. Major Petrochemical Feedstocks

Important feedstocks include:

  • Naphtha.
  • Ethane.
  • Propane.
  • Butane.
  • Natural gas.
  • Refinery gases.
67. Steam Cracking
  • Steam cracking produces small unsaturated hydrocarbons.
  • Feedstocks such as ethane or naphtha are heated strongly with steam.
  • Major products include ethylene and propylene.
  • These are basic building blocks for plastics.
68. Ethylene
  • Ethylene is also called ethene.
  • Formula → C₂H₄.
  • It is an alkene.
  • It is used to manufacture polyethylene.
  • Ethylene is also a natural plant hormone involved in fruit ripening.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ethene → C₂H₄ → Polyethylene

69. Propylene
  • Propylene is also called propene.
  • Formula → C₃H₆.
  • It is used to manufacture polypropylene.
  • It is an important petrochemical feedstock.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Propene → C₃H₆ → Polypropylene

70. Polyethylene
  • Polyethylene is produced by polymerisation of ethylene.
  • It is one of the most widely used plastics.
  • It is used in bags, containers, pipes and packaging.
71. Polypropylene
  • Polypropylene is produced from propylene.
  • It is used in packaging, fibres, household items and automobile components.
  • It is relatively lightweight and chemically resistant.
72. PVC
  • PVC stands for Polyvinyl Chloride.
  • Its monomer is vinyl chloride.
  • PVC is used in pipes, cable insulation, flooring and construction materials.
  • Chlorine is present in PVC's chemical structure.
73. Polystyrene
  • Polystyrene is produced from styrene.
  • It is used in packaging, insulation and disposable products.
  • Expanded polystyrene contains many gas-filled cells.
74. Synthetic Rubber
  • Several synthetic rubbers are produced from petrochemical feedstocks.
  • Examples include styrene-butadiene rubber and neoprene.
  • Synthetic rubber is widely used in tyres and industrial goods.
75. Synthetic Fibres from Petrochemicals

Examples include:

  • Nylon.
  • Polyester.
  • Acrylic fibres.
  • Many textile fibres therefore originate ultimately from petroleum or natural-gas feedstocks.
76. Detergents
  • Synthetic detergents are largely produced from petrochemical raw materials.
  • They contain surfactants.
  • Surfactants reduce surface tension and help remove grease.
77. Solvents

Petroleum-derived solvents include:

  • Hexane.
  • Toluene.
  • Xylene.
  • Mineral spirits.
  • They are used in paints, cleaning and chemical manufacturing.
  • Many are flammable and require careful handling.
78. Natural Gas
  • Natural gas is a fossil fuel.
  • Methane is its major component.
  • It may also contain ethane, propane, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and traces of other gases.
  • Natural gas is generally cleaner-burning than coal and heavy fuel oil.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Natural Gas → Mainly Methane

79. Methane
  • Formula → CH₄.
  • It is the simplest alkane.
  • It is colourless.
  • Pure methane is odourless.
  • It burns to form carbon dioxide and water under complete combustion.
📌 Reaction

CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

80. Complete Combustion

For a hydrocarbon with sufficient oxygen:

Hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + Energy

  • Complete combustion releases heat.
  • Carbon dioxide and water are major products.
81. Incomplete Combustion
  • In limited oxygen, hydrocarbons may form carbon monoxide.
  • Soot or elemental carbon may also form.
  • Incomplete combustion releases less usable energy.
  • Carbon monoxide is highly poisonous.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Insufficient O₂ → CO + Soot Possible

82. Carbon Monoxide
  • Carbon monoxide formula is CO.
  • It is colourless and odourless.
  • It forms during incomplete combustion.
  • It binds strongly with haemoglobin.
  • It reduces oxygen transport in blood.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CO → Incomplete Combustion → Poisonous

83. CNG
  • CNG stands for Compressed Natural Gas.
  • It consists mainly of methane.
  • Natural gas is compressed to high pressure for vehicle storage.
  • CNG generally produces lower particulate emissions than diesel.
  • It is used as an automobile fuel.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CNG → Compressed Natural Gas → Mainly CH₄

84. LNG
  • LNG stands for Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • Natural gas is cooled to very low temperature until it becomes liquid.
  • LNG occupies far less volume than gas.
  • It enables efficient long-distance transport, especially by ship.
  • LNG is stored cryogenically.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LNG → Natural Gas Liquefied by Cooling

85. CNG vs LNG
  • CNG → Gas compressed under high pressure.
  • LNG → Gas liquefied by very low temperature.
  • Both consist mainly of methane.
  • CNG is common in road transport.
  • LNG is important for bulk storage and transport.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

CNG → Compression.

LNG → Cooling/Liquefaction.

86. LPG vs CNG
  • LPG mainly contains propane and butane.
  • CNG mainly contains methane.
  • LPG is stored as liquid under pressure.
  • CNG is stored mainly as highly compressed gas.
  • They are different fuels.
📌 Must-Memorise

LPG → Propane + Butane

CNG → Methane

87. Biogas vs Natural Gas
  • Both can contain large amounts of methane.
  • Natural gas is a fossil fuel.
  • Biogas forms from anaerobic decomposition of recent organic matter.
  • Raw biogas often contains substantial carbon dioxide.
  • Purified biomethane can resemble natural gas in composition.
88. Calorific Value
  • Calorific value is the heat released by complete combustion of a unit quantity of fuel.
  • For solid and liquid fuels, it is often expressed in kJ/kg or MJ/kg.
  • For gases, values may also be expressed per unit volume.
  • Higher calorific value means more heat released per unit fuel under specified conditions.
89. Petroleum Fuels and Energy Density
  • Petroleum fuels have high energy density.
  • This makes them convenient for transport.
  • Liquid fuels are easy to store and pump.
  • Their high energy density helped dominate road, air and marine transport.
90. Combustion of Sulfur
  • Sulfur in fuel burns to produce sulfur dioxide.
  • SO₂ contributes to air pollution.
  • It can form acids in the atmosphere.
  • Fuel desulfurisation reduces these emissions.
📌 Reaction

S + O₂ → SO₂

91. Nitrogen Oxides
  • High-temperature combustion can produce nitrogen oxides.
  • NO and NO₂ are collectively important NOₓ pollutants.
  • NOₓ contributes to photochemical smog and acid deposition.
  • Vehicle emission-control systems reduce NOₓ.
92. Particulate Matter
  • Diesel combustion can produce soot and fine particles.
  • Modern diesel engines use fuel injection and after-treatment systems to reduce particulate emissions.
  • Fine particulate matter adversely affects respiratory and cardiovascular health.
93. Carbon Dioxide and Petroleum
  • Combustion of petroleum fuels releases CO₂.
  • CO₂ is a greenhouse gas.
  • Fossil-fuel combustion is a major anthropogenic source of carbon dioxide.
  • Improved fuel efficiency can reduce emissions per unit of useful work.
94. Volatile Organic Compounds
  • Petrol vapours contain volatile organic compounds.
  • VOCs contribute to air pollution and photochemical smog.
  • Vapour-recovery systems reduce emissions during fuel handling.
95. Photochemical Smog
  • Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.
  • Ground-level ozone is an important component.
  • Vehicle emissions are major contributors in urban areas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

NOₓ + VOC + Sunlight → Photochemical Smog

96. Catalytic Converter
  • Catalytic converters are installed in vehicle exhaust systems.
  • They convert harmful gases into less harmful products.
  • Carbon monoxide can be oxidised to carbon dioxide.
  • Unburned hydrocarbons can be oxidised.
  • Nitrogen oxides can be reduced to nitrogen in three-way catalytic systems.
  • Platinum-group metals are common catalysts.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Catalytic Converter → Vehicle Emission Control

97. Catalytic Converter Metals

Important catalytic metals include:

  • Platinum.
  • Palladium.
  • Rhodium.
  • They catalyse oxidation and reduction reactions in exhaust gas.
98. Petrol Evaporation
  • Petrol evaporates rapidly because it contains volatile hydrocarbons.
  • Therefore, petrol containers must be tightly closed.
  • Petrol vapour mixed with air is highly flammable.
99. Diesel Volatility
  • Diesel is much less volatile than petrol.
  • It has a higher flash point.
  • This contributes to different storage and ignition behaviour.
100. Petroleum as Non-Renewable Resource
  • Petroleum reserves are finite.
  • Formation takes geological timescales.
  • Human consumption occurs far faster than natural formation.
  • Petroleum therefore cannot be considered renewable.
101. Petroleum Conservation

Conservation measures include:

  • Improving vehicle fuel efficiency.
  • Using public transport.
  • Avoiding unnecessary idling.
  • Maintaining correct tyre pressure.
  • Reducing fuel leakage and wastage.
  • Using alternative energy where practical.
  • Recycling petrochemical materials.
102. Petroleum Spills
  • Oil spills contaminate marine and coastal environments.
  • Oil can coat birds and marine organisms.
  • It can reduce oxygen exchange and damage habitats.
  • Cleanup methods include booms, skimmers, absorbents and controlled remediation.
103. Refinery Pollution

Potential refinery pollutants include:

  • Sulfur compounds.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • VOCs.
  • Particulate matter.
  • Wastewater.
  • Carbon dioxide.
  • Modern refineries use pollution-control systems.
104. Crude-Oil Desalting
  • Crude oil can contain water and dissolved salts.
  • Desalting removes salt and water before major refining.
  • This reduces corrosion and deposits in refinery equipment.
105. Petroleum Coke
  • Petroleum coke is a carbon-rich solid obtained from heavy petroleum residues.
  • It is produced in coking processes.
  • It is used as industrial fuel and carbon material.
  • Some grades have high sulfur content.
106. Coking
  • Coking converts heavy residual oil into lighter products and solid petroleum coke.
  • It is a thermal cracking process.
  • It helps process very heavy refinery residues.
107. Wax Removal
  • Lubricating-oil fractions may contain waxes.
  • Dewaxing improves low-temperature flow properties.
  • Paraffin wax can be recovered as a useful product.
108. Pour Point
  • Pour point is the lowest temperature at which an oil remains able to flow under specified test conditions.
  • It is important for lubricants and diesel fuels in cold climates.
109. Cloud Point
  • Cloud point is the temperature at which wax crystals first become visibly apparent in certain petroleum products.
  • It is important for diesel and lubricating oils in cold conditions.
110. Lubricant Viscosity
  • Lubricant must maintain suitable viscosity.
  • If too thin, it may not maintain a protective film.
  • If too thick, it increases resistance and energy loss.
  • Viscosity changes with temperature.
111. Viscosity Index
  • Viscosity index indicates how strongly a lubricant's viscosity changes with temperature.
  • Higher viscosity index means relatively smaller viscosity change with temperature.
  • It is important in engine oils.
112. Petrol Additives

Petrol may contain additives to:

  • Improve detergency.
  • Control deposits.
  • Improve stability.
  • Increase octane performance.
  • Reduce corrosion.
113. Diesel Additives

Diesel additives can:

  • Improve cetane quality.
  • Improve lubricity.
  • Control deposits.
  • Improve cold-flow properties.
  • Reduce oxidation during storage.
114. Biofuel Blending
  • Ethanol can be blended with petrol.
  • Biodiesel can be blended with petroleum diesel.
  • Blending can reduce petroleum consumption.
  • Fuel properties and engine compatibility must meet specifications.
115. Ethanol
  • Ethanol formula is C₂H₅OH.
  • It can be produced by fermentation or industrial chemical routes.
  • It contains oxygen in its molecule.
  • Ethanol is blended with petrol in many countries.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ethanol → Petrol Blending

116. Gasohol
  • Gasohol is a mixture of petrol and ethanol.
  • The exact ethanol percentage can vary.
  • It reduces use of pure fossil petrol.
  • Ethanol contributes oxygen to the fuel mixture.
117. Biodiesel
  • Biodiesel consists mainly of fatty-acid esters produced from vegetable oils, animal fats or other lipid sources.
  • It is not a petroleum product itself.
  • It can be blended with petroleum diesel.
  • It is renewable when produced from renewable biological feedstocks.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Biodiesel ≠ Petroleum diesel, though they can be blended.

118. Hydrogen as Fuel — Comparison
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a petroleum product.
  • Combustion of hydrogen produces water.
  • Hydrogen can also be used in fuel cells.
  • Its climate benefit depends on how the hydrogen is produced.
119. Petrochemical Fertiliser Link
  • Natural gas is a major source of hydrogen for ammonia production.
  • Ammonia is used to manufacture nitrogen fertilisers.
  • Therefore, natural gas is indirectly important to fertiliser production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Natural Gas → H₂ → NH₃ → Fertilisers

120. Petrochemical Plastics Link
  • Ethylene → Polyethylene.
  • Propylene → Polypropylene.
  • Styrene → Polystyrene.
  • Vinyl chloride → PVC.
  • Petroleum and natural gas are therefore major raw materials for plastics.
121. Petroleum in Pharmaceuticals
  • Petrochemical feedstocks are used to manufacture many solvents, intermediates and synthetic materials used by pharmaceutical industries.
  • Petroleum is therefore important beyond fuel production.
122. Petroleum in Cosmetics
  • Petroleum-derived materials can be used in cosmetics.
  • Petroleum jelly is a common example.
  • Paraffin and mineral oils are also used in selected formulations after purification.
123. Mineral Oil
  • Mineral oil is a purified mixture of liquid hydrocarbons derived from petroleum.
  • It has applications in lubrication, pharmaceuticals and cosmetics depending on purity grade.
124. Indian Petroleum — Digboi
  • Digboi is located in Assam.
  • It is one of the oldest oil-producing centres in India.
  • Petroleum development at Digboi began during the nineteenth century.
  • Digboi became historically important in India's petroleum industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Digboi → Assam → Early Indian Petroleum Centre

125. Digboi Refinery
  • Digboi Refinery in Assam is one of India's oldest operating refineries.
  • It began operation in the early twentieth century.
  • Digboi is frequently asked in competitive examinations in relation to early Indian petroleum history.
126. Mumbai High
  • Mumbai High is a major offshore oil field in the Arabian Sea.
  • It lies off the western coast of India.
  • Its discovery greatly increased India's domestic petroleum production.
  • Offshore production is an important part of India's oil industry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mumbai High → Offshore Oil Field → Arabian Sea

127. Assam Oil Fields

Important petroleum areas of Assam include:

  • Digboi.
  • Naharkatiya.
  • Moran.
  • Assam is historically one of India's major petroleum-producing regions.
128. Gujarat Petroleum Region
  • Gujarat has important oil and natural-gas fields.
  • Ankleshwar is a well-known oil field.
  • Cambay or Khambhat Basin contains hydrocarbon resources.
  • Gujarat is an important refining and petrochemical state.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ankleshwar → Gujarat → Petroleum

129. Cauvery Basin
  • The Cauvery Basin contains oil and natural-gas resources.
  • It extends across parts of Tamil Nadu and adjoining offshore regions.
  • Hydrocarbon exploration and production occur in the basin.
  • The basin is important for Tamil Nadu-focused geography and economy questions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamil Nadu Petroleum → Cauvery Basin

130. Narimanam
  • Narimanam in the Cauvery Basin of Tamil Nadu is associated with petroleum production.
  • It lies in the Nagapattinam region.
  • It is an important Tamil Nadu petroleum-location fact for competitive examinations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Narimanam → Tamil Nadu → Petroleum

131. Chennai Petroleum Refining
  • Chennai has major petroleum-refining activity.
  • Manali in north Chennai is an important refinery and petrochemical location.
  • Petroleum refining supports fuel supply and downstream industries in Tamil Nadu.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Manali, Chennai → Petroleum Refining

132. Petroleum Conservation Research Association
  • Petroleum conservation campaigns in India have focused on efficient use of petroleum fuels.
  • Public awareness has historically encouraged fuel saving in transport, homes and industry.
  • Conservation reduces import dependence and emissions.
133. Strategic Petroleum Reserves
  • Strategic petroleum reserves store crude oil for emergency supply disruptions.
  • They provide energy-security support.
  • Such reserves are separate from ordinary commercial stocks.
134. Petroleum Imports
  • India consumes more crude petroleum than it produces domestically.
  • Imported crude therefore plays a major role in India's energy supply.
  • This makes petroleum conservation and diversification of energy sources economically important.
135. Petroleum and Transport

Petroleum products dominate many transport uses:

  • Petrol → Spark-ignition road vehicles.
  • Diesel → Compression-ignition vehicles.
  • ATF → Jet aircraft.
  • Fuel oil/diesel → Marine and industrial uses.
136. Important Full Forms
  • LPG → Liquefied Petroleum Gas.
  • CNG → Compressed Natural Gas.
  • LNG → Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • ATF → Aviation Turbine Fuel.
  • FCC → Fluid Catalytic Cracking.
  • VOC → Volatile Organic Compound.
137. Must-Memorise Product–Use Pairs
  • LPG → Cooking.
  • Petrol → Spark-ignition vehicles.
  • Kerosene → Stove/aviation-fuel base.
  • Diesel → Compression-ignition engines.
  • Lubricating oil → Machinery.
  • Paraffin wax → Candles.
  • Bitumen → Roads.
  • Naphtha → Petrochemicals.
  • CNG → Vehicle fuel.
  • LNG → Bulk natural-gas transport.
138. Must-Memorise Fuel Comparisons
  • Petrol → More volatile.
  • Diesel → Less volatile.
  • Petrol → Lower flash point.
  • Diesel → Higher flash point.
  • Petrol engine → Spark ignition.
  • Diesel engine → Compression ignition.
  • Petrol quality → Octane number.
  • Diesel quality → Cetane number.
139. Must-Memorise Petrochemical Links
  • Methane → Natural gas.
  • Ethene → Polyethylene.
  • Propene → Polypropylene.
  • Vinyl chloride → PVC.
  • Styrene → Polystyrene.
  • Naphtha → Petrochemical feedstock.
140. TNPSC Traps
  • Petroleum is a mixture, not a single compound.
  • Petroleum contains mainly hydrocarbons.
  • Petroleum is non-renewable.
  • Refining is not the same as simply boiling crude oil once.
  • Fractional distillation separates according to boiling ranges.
  • Light fractions condense higher in the column.
  • Heavy fractions condense lower.
  • LPG mainly contains propane and butane.
  • CNG mainly contains methane.
  • LPG and CNG are not the same.
  • LNG is produced mainly by cooling natural gas.
  • CNG is produced mainly by compression.
  • Petrol is more volatile than diesel.
  • Diesel has a higher flash point than petrol.
  • Petrol engines use spark ignition.
  • Diesel engines use compression ignition.
  • Octane number belongs to petrol.
  • Cetane number belongs to diesel.
  • High octane means high knock resistance, not necessarily higher energy content.
  • Iso-octane reference value → 100.
  • n-Heptane reference value → 0.
  • Cracking breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller ones.
  • Reforming improves petrol octane quality.
  • Desulfurisation reduces sulfur pollution.
  • Sweet crude contains less sulfur.
  • Sour crude contains more sulfur.
  • Bitumen is a heavy refinery residue.
  • Paraffin wax comes from petroleum.
  • Petroleum jelly comes from petroleum.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane.
  • CO forms from incomplete combustion.
  • SO₂ forms from sulfur-containing fuel combustion.
  • NOₓ forms mainly at high combustion temperatures.
  • Catalytic converters reduce vehicle pollutants.
  • Biodiesel is not a petroleum product.
  • Ethanol is commonly blended with petrol.
  • Digboi is in Assam.
  • Mumbai High is an offshore oil field in the Arabian Sea.
  • Cauvery Basin is important for Tamil Nadu hydrocarbons.
  • Narimanam is associated with petroleum production in Tamil Nadu.
141. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Petroleum → Fossil fuel.
  • Petroleum → Hydrocarbons.
  • Refining → Fractional distillation.
  • Top fraction → LPG.
  • Bottom → Bitumen.
  • LPG → Propane + butane.
  • Petrol → Spark ignition.
  • Diesel → Compression ignition.
  • Petrol → Octane.
  • Diesel → Cetane.
  • Iso-octane → 100.
  • n-Heptane → 0.
  • Naphtha → Petrochemicals.
  • Kerosene → Jet-fuel base.
  • Lubricant → Friction ↓.
  • Paraffin → Candles.
  • Bitumen → Roads.
  • Cracking → Large to small.
  • Reforming → Octane ↑.
  • Sweet crude → Low sulfur.
  • Sour crude → High sulfur.
  • Natural gas → Methane.
  • CNG → Compressed methane-rich gas.
  • LNG → Liquefied by cooling.
  • CO → Incomplete combustion.
  • Catalytic converter → Pollution control.
  • Digboi → Assam.
  • Mumbai High → Arabian Sea.
  • Cauvery Basin → Tamil Nadu petroleum.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Petroleum is what type of substance? → Complex mixture of hydrocarbons.
  • Is petroleum renewable? → No.
  • Petroleum formed mainly from? → Ancient organic matter subjected to heat and pressure.
  • Three major fossil fuels? → Coal, petroleum and natural gas.
  • What is crude oil? → Unrefined petroleum obtained from reservoirs.
  • Main elements in hydrocarbons? → Carbon and hydrogen.
  • Major refinery separation process? → Fractional distillation.
  • Basis of fractional distillation? → Different boiling ranges.
  • Fractionating column temperature? → Hotter at bottom, cooler at top.
  • Light petroleum fractions collected where? → Near the top.
  • Heavy fractions collected where? → Near the bottom.
  • Lightest major refinery product group? → Refinery gases/LPG.
  • Heavy refinery residue used on roads? → Bitumen.
  • LPG stands for? → Liquefied Petroleum Gas.
  • Main components of LPG? → Propane and butane.
  • Why is LPG liquefied? → Easier storage in smaller volume.
  • Why does domestic LPG have a strong smell? → Odorant is deliberately added.
  • Is pure LPG naturally strongly odorous? → No.
  • Petrol is also called? → Gasoline.
  • Which is more volatile, petrol or diesel? → Petrol.
  • Petrol is mainly used in? → Spark-ignition engines.
  • Diesel used in? → Compression-ignition engines.
  • Does a normal diesel engine require a spark plug for ignition? → No.
  • Petroleum fraction used as major petrochemical feedstock? → Naphtha.
  • Kerosene used as base for? → Aviation turbine fuel.
  • ATF stands for? → Aviation Turbine Fuel.
  • Lubricating oil function? → Reduce friction and wear.
  • Paraffin wax commonly used in? → Candles.
  • Bitumen commonly used in? → Road construction.
  • General trend down fractionating column? → Molecular size, boiling point and viscosity increase.
  • General trend in volatility downward? → Decreases.
  • Flash point means? → Lowest temperature at which vapour ignites briefly.
  • Which generally has higher flash point, diesel or petrol? → Diesel.
  • Fire point means? → Temperature at which burning can continue.
  • Octane number refers to? → Petrol anti-knock quality.
  • Higher octane means? → Greater resistance to knocking.
  • Traditional octane reference assigned 100? → Iso-octane.
  • Reference assigned 0? → n-Heptane.
  • Cetane number refers to? → Diesel ignition quality.
  • Petrol quality number? → Octane.
  • Diesel quality number? → Cetane.
  • Historic anti-knock additive in petrol? → Tetraethyl lead.
  • Why was leaded petrol phased out? → Health and environmental toxicity.
  • Cracking means? → Breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller hydrocarbons.
  • Two broad cracking types? → Thermal and catalytic cracking.
  • FCC stands for? → Fluid Catalytic Cracking.
  • Hydrocracking uses? → Hydrogen and catalyst.
  • Reforming does what? → Improves petrol octane quality by rearranging hydrocarbons.
  • Isomerisation converts? → Straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched isomers.
  • Purpose of desulfurisation? → Remove sulfur from fuels.
  • Why remove sulfur? → Reduce SO₂ emissions.
  • Sweet crude means? → Low-sulfur crude.
  • Sour crude means? → Higher-sulfur crude.
  • Petrochemicals are obtained mainly from? → Petroleum and natural gas.
  • Major petrochemical raw material from refinery? → Naphtha.
  • Ethene formula? → C₂H₄.
  • Ethene produces? → Polyethylene.
  • Propene formula? → C₃H₆.
  • Propene produces? → Polypropylene.
  • PVC stands for? → Polyvinyl Chloride.
  • Natural gas main component? → Methane.
  • Methane formula? → CH₄.
  • Complete methane combustion products? → CO₂ and H₂O.
  • Incomplete combustion can produce? → Carbon monoxide and soot.
  • Why is CO dangerous? → It binds strongly with haemoglobin.
  • CNG stands for? → Compressed Natural Gas.
  • Main component of CNG? → Methane.
  • LNG stands for? → Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • How is CNG stored? → By high-pressure compression.
  • How is LNG produced? → By cooling natural gas until liquid.
  • LPG vs CNG composition? → LPG mainly propane/butane; CNG mainly methane.
  • Is biogas a fossil fuel? → No.
  • Calorific value means? → Heat released by complete combustion of unit quantity of fuel.
  • Sulfur in fuel forms? → Sulfur dioxide.
  • NOₓ formed mainly because of? → High-temperature combustion.
  • Photochemical smog involves? → NOₓ, VOCs and sunlight.
  • Device reducing vehicle exhaust pollutants? → Catalytic converter.
  • Common catalytic-converter metals? → Platinum, palladium and rhodium.
  • CO₂ from petroleum combustion is what type of gas? → Greenhouse gas.
  • Petroleum coke obtained from? → Heavy refinery residues.
  • Coking produces? → Lighter hydrocarbons + petroleum coke.
  • Ethanol commonly blended with? → Petrol.
  • Gasohol means? → Petrol–ethanol blend.
  • Biodiesel comes mainly from? → Biological oils/fats.
  • Is biodiesel itself petroleum diesel? → No.
  • Natural gas important in fertiliser industry because it provides? → Hydrogen for ammonia production.
  • Important early petroleum centre in India? → Digboi.
  • Digboi is in? → Assam.
  • Important offshore oil field of India? → Mumbai High.
  • Mumbai High lies in? → Arabian Sea.
  • Ankleshwar oil field is in? → Gujarat.
  • Important hydrocarbon basin in Tamil Nadu? → Cauvery Basin.
  • Tamil Nadu petroleum location commonly asked? → Narimanam.
  • Important petroleum-refining area in Chennai? → Manali.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Petroleum → fractional distillation; LPG → propane + butane; Petrol → octane/spark ignition; Diesel → cetane/compression ignition; Naphtha → petrochemicals; Bitumen → roads; Natural gas/CNG → methane.
